item.content:encoded:
Continuing the ongoing series of interviews with creative artists working on various aspects of movie and TV productions, it is my pleasure to welcome Nick Bassett. In this interview, he talks the role of production design and the bigger changes in the art department in the last few decades, key ingredients to longevity in the industry, experiencing stories on the big screen, and the enduring appeal of the horror genre. Between all these and more, Nick takes a deep dive into his work on “Insidious: Out Of The Further”.

Kirill: Please tell us about yourself and the path that took you to where you are today.

Nick: I was always quite good at art from a young age. Later on I went to an all-boys high school, and while I did fine there, their art department was pretty terrible. I ended up switching to a different high school, and their art department was great. They had an option to take it as two subjects, which was a rare occurrence for local high schools.

That was a memorable year for me, and from there I decided to do either fine arts or a design school. I chose an industrial design school, and in some ways I looked at that with a bit of regret. It’s such a luxury to be able to do pure art and indulge in that. For some reason, there was a slightly more cautious side of me that advised that I should go down a path of something that may lead to a career, rather than just a freelance artist. About 2.5 years into the 4 year program I decided it wasn’t for me. While I liked it overall, I just wasn’t learning much. I felt a need to go and do something practical.

One of the part time tutors at the school was designing furniture, making jewelry and other bespoke things. He was a trained jeweler, but not a trained furniture designer, and that triggered my imagination that there is a world where you can just go out and do this thing. I worked with him for a while and learned about jewelry, welding, metal casting and other practical things. Along the way there was a small opportunity to make props. That was my first introduction to the world of TV commercials, and from there through word of mouth I discovered the existence of the film industry.

I always wanted to do my own design and my own products. I might have had lofty ideas of being like Philippe Starck, some superstar designer [laughs]. Everyone at design school thinks they’re going to be the next big thing, and that’s kind of mad to think when you have so much global competition.

I probably had a few opportunities where I could get into the film industry. One was through TV commercials, and the other was where I’ve met people who are making props in the old fashioned way. They make fake giant ice creams and closeups of pouring fake chocolate for beautiful Cadbury ads. It’s really detailed work and they were working at such a precision level.

And then this one weekend I was up at my family home, and this red Ford Mustang pulled up outside my mum’s house. I look outside, and I see a camera crew, and they were making an episode of the TV show called “High Tide”. People were wearing Hawaiian shirts, as that episode was supposed to be set in Hawaii. That moment was a trigger for me, as it looked so fun. My partner at the time, who is my wife now, had been offered a running job on that show, and while she turned it down, she asked me if I wanted to take it. That was it, and I thank her for it.

It gave me the very bottom rung as an art department runner – with the potential that you could see that you could move all the way up to doing production design. The head people in that art department were trained architects, and that was so interesting. I could see a path where it wasn’t going to be a dead end.

I then worked my way all the way through, and I’ve been doing this now for 30+ years. I went from running to set dressing to standby working on the floor of the set. And then back into the art department, after earning my way back through – and always doing design projects on my own on the side. That was all in New Zealand. The industry was quite new there. There’s always been a film and TV industry, but it was very small, and you had these American projects coming in. Everyone was putting on American accents for these superstar actors [laughs]. It was a major trigger to your imagination to work on a detective show set in California or Hawaii or some other place that wasn’t local.

It took about 8 years for me to find my way to the film industry. I was 17 when I went to design school, about 21 when I first heard about this industry, and 25 when I realized that it was a career that you could stick with. There’s no straight path in the film industry. It’s one of those jobs with no promises or guarantees.


On the sets of “Insidious: Out Of The Further”, courtesy of Nick Bassett and Sony Pictures.

Kirill: As you look at these 30 years that you’ve been doing this, you’ve probably seen quite a few changes in and around the art department. What would you say are the bigger changes?

Nick: When I was starting out, everything was hand drawn, and now it’s all in 3D computer programs. On some of the smaller shows back then it was just sketches and no working drawings [laughs]. The scale of every movie is different, but the basic practice now is a lot more. We’re having to document what we do a lot more and sell the concept, so we can share it with other departments.

The best time you’ll ever have is when you start in the film industry because you don’t know anything. When you know more, it gets harder, because now you realize what you didn’t know. I imagine there’s very few people who feel like experts in our industry, because there’s so much to learn all the time and no two projects are the same. You’re always learning, and you’re always feeling like there’s more to learn.

We have a better understanding of the importance of color, of how the costume works with the backdrop, and how all departments interlace. I often work on horror shows, and you have so many departments that have to mesh together. It’s a really big responsibility to communicate clearly and to leave a documented trail of what we’ve decided to do to prevent surprises on the day. Our industry in New Zealand has seen a massive change since back then. We learned from overseas crews that were coming in, and now in New Zealand you see a much more professional department that takes it seriously.

It’s a competitive industry, and one that has matured quite a bit. A lot of people want to be in it. A lot of countries are competing for work. So everyone needs to be really good at what they’re doing. You can’t relax in it too much.

Technology is coming in more and more, but it’s always been there. Everyone has always been progressing. I started back in the days of film, and then digital started coming in, and we were learning how digital cameras are different from film cameras. They were much cleaner, and they were picking up detail that we wouldn’t have noticed before. That was a long time ago now, but it’s just another example of how you’re constantly training your brain to cope with technology changes.

Now we’re in a much faster tracked prep period. Our pre-production period is very quick now. It’s not enough to be good at it. You also have to be fast and efficient, and do work with fewer people. There’s nothing stable about it. It keeps evolving. I like to embrace technology as much as possible. One thing I do is I stay with the basics. I try not to jump ahead of myself. Technology can quickly get you something that looks finished and resolved, all the while you still have to go through the creative stages.


On the sets of “Insidious: Out Of The Further”, courtesy of Nick Bassett and Sony Pictures.

Kirill: What are the bigger misconceptions or misunderstandings about what production design is?

Nick: In a way, it’s quite easy to explain production design. But then you have multiple departments on bigger projects with visual effects, special effects and in-camera work that are creating worlds, and it’s possibly easy to think that the production designer is responsible for all of that. But of course there are high ranking and experienced people within each department that we integrate with – extending to costume, make-up and others.

The best description of my job is that we build a robust world. If we’re doing a fantasy, I present as many images that will help tell a story and give all the other departments everything they need to do their job. It’s almost an endless task, but at no point do you take credit for all of the hard work, because everyone is contributing their part. I happen to be the head of the department that starts earliest, and then people come into it, and it keeps building.

If you’re outside the industry, none of it might make any sense to you. When I say I’m a production designer and I explain what goes into it, people ask me to explain it again and again. If I say that I’m responsible for designing the set, they ask why don’t you just film in real places [laughs]. It takes a long time to explain that 90% of what we’re seeing on camera is created and painted, even if it’s a small piece of it.

This job is about leadership and motivation. You’re pushing your own department as far as you can with the resources you have to give as much information and answer as many questions for other people starting. I love it when other people grab hold of things and run as well and we’re all working together. When you get the script, we’re trying to push this locomotive to get it moving. We’re trying to get ideas and build sets and design everything. And once it starts moving, you have to try and outrun this thing – because the momentum of a film with its schedule is a powerful thing.

Another part of the production design job which is not spoken about as much is that we’re involved with very early decisions. Are we going to rent soundstages? Are we going to shoot on location? What are we going to build? What is this going to cost? What countries are we going to film? You go with your gut instinct so often, and these decisions then inform the budget of the whole project. It’s an exciting moment when you read a script and see a problem that you have to crack. Some things are not as easy to solve as others. The logistics of it is like a jigsaw puzzle that we’re solving together.

What can we cram into these sound stages? How can we turn them around and how are we going to work with the producers to give them what they need before all the other crews start? It’s a hidden part of the job, and people may not understand how mechanical a lot of it is at the beginning. You break them down methodically, and in some ways these become the interesting challenges.

Kirill: Getting to “Insidious”, how did it find its way to you, or maybe how did you find your way to it?

Nick: “Insidious” was a Blumhouse project, and they do a lot of joint projects with Atomic Monster. I was working on Lee Cronin’s “The Mummy” in Dublin, which is another Atomic Monster production. Dave Garbett was the cinematographer on it, and we’ve worked together a lot in the past. His name came up for “Insidious”, and then my name came up in the mix as well.

I had a Zoom call with the director. You read the script, you put some ideas together – not necessarily visuals, but more of your thoughts on what we can talk about during the call. Jacob Chase the director has seen some of my earlier work, and we had a common love of the same projects. So I ended up wrapping one movie in Dublin, then home for a week, and then to Melbourne to make “Insidious”.


On the sets of “Insidious: Out Of The Further”, courtesy of Nick Bassett and Sony Pictures.

Kirill: I’m not sure how it is in the rest of the world, New Zealand included, but it feels that Americans love horror movies – going back decades all the way not just to the ’70s, but to early black-and-white ’30s. How do you explain this phenomenon of the evergreen obsession with the horror genre?

Nick: For me it’s quite simple. The closest thing to it is a rollercoaster ride or going to a theme park. If you want to have a night out and have a lot of laughs, you go to a horror movie. Horror and comedy are quite closely interwoven, and they evoke similar emotions. If you want to experience something intense for a short period of time, horror is a really good way to do it.

I find that horror fans are quite forgiving of bad horror, if you will. They like the genre and they’ll go anyway. People go to horror movies with their mates. People go to horror movies on a date. Many people take horror seriously, but for the average person it’s just a laugh. They’re normally often absurd. It’s something crazy and ridiculous – but you can watch it, laugh at it, cry at it, or jump at it, or whatever. You experience this emotional range, and then hop off that rollercoaster ride, and still have time for dinner.

It appeals to people who want a short blast of excitement, and other movies don’t promise that. Superhero movies can deliver it in ways, but that often involves a lot more buy-in or a more extreme world building. Horror can boil down to something very simple. “Insidious” has this simple idea of this gateway to the Further. You can get into the groove of it quite quickly. And it’s usually moving at a good pace.

You’re on this theme park ride. You hop on this ride with your friends, you have this journey, and you can talk about it afterwards. It’s generally not overly complicated, and you can all get it. It’s a lot of fun for filmmakers. We know what we’re trying to do. We’re trying to make a fun ride.

Kirill: This is the sixth installment in the “Insidious” franchise. Do you feel that there’s a certain expectation from the audience in how this world is “supposed” to look like?

Nick: This franchise is quite carefully guarded. Jacob came up with a new idea for it, but you have James Wan, Leigh Whannell and Jason Blum all involved, and everybody is aware of the fan base for the project. There is a version where we could have taken the story and changed everything. There is a bit of a time gap from the last one, but you don’t want to suddenly start so fresh that people are confused about what that franchise is.

There’s an expectation to change and develop and progress, but we certainly didn’t want to take for granted the fact that it has a big fan base. Jacob knows all these movies intimately. He knew every detail of the previous films. At that point, I have a lot of trust in the director, because they have been involved in many conversations before I started.

We wanted this one to be a bit of fun to see all these characters from previous movies come back, to celebrate the franchise a little bit, and then to bring a new idea to it – but not bring so many ideas that it felt like a different franchise. You have a spectrum of fans, and I’ve seen this through my involvement in the “Evil Dead” movies and TV shows. Some fans love the humor in it, and some fans hate it. You’ll never please everyone.

Jacob wrote a great script for “Insidious”, and everyone loved the idea. We tried to make the best movie we could make, and honor the previous films, and not have it feel totally disconnected. We are aware that we’re introducing new characters, and it’s a challenge. We had 10 weeks for pre-production, and a lot of things were happening quickly.


On the set of the pillow fort tunnels of “Insidious: Out Of The Further”, courtesy of Nick Bassett and Sony Pictures.

Kirill: The main character Gemma spends her time between the cluttered house and open, spacious dental clinic. How did you approach thinking about these two spaces?

Nick: I gather as many references at the beginning of the movie as possible. Then I lay the movie out on a board in its chronological order and look for moments. Color is one moment. Space is another moment. As you’re saying, one moment can be claustrophobic, and then the next can be more open or sparse. The dentist office is the extremely opposite to her family home which was damp, dark, and depressing in some ways. One version of that family house is quite warm, if you turn all the lights on. But we saw it as dim and heavy, and the opposite to the clean and clinical world of her workplace.

And then we’re bringing in the Further concept, so we wanted spaces that can open up and be something else that she falls into. Some of those decisions are 100% creative as a look, and others have practical ramifications that you have to consider.

When she came back to turn her childhood home into a family home for her and her daughter, we didn’t want to completely remodel it and lose some of the character we had earlier. It was a more realistic renovation – a lot of paint rather than knocking walls down. We tried to do it in a way that we felt was believable. You’re creating your own backstory. You read the script, and there’s a scene here and a scene here – but there’s not a lot of description of what happened in the middle. What happened in the 20 years that we don’t have in our movie?

Our job as an art department is to build that backstory. We’re always talking about these moments that will help us get to what that look is in creating our own story. It’s a lot of fun. You’re essentially writing your own script to fill in the blanks and checking it with the director. We’re trying to put ourselves in that situation as designers. What would be the history of it? What part of America are they in? What’s the climate like? What’s the school like? What can we add to build more of a backstory?

You may not see it on screen in detail every time. One interesting thing with horror is that the camera is always moving past things, and you never know where that camera’s going to land. A shot might be designed in a certain way, and then suddenly it’s revolving around some random part of the set, and it’s going to be huge on screen. I want to detail everything correctly. I’m obsessed about every little corner of the set.

There’s a common saying in the industry that people don’t notice these details, and if they do, you’ve lost them as the viewer. But I believe that the details are the key to it. You may not scrutinize the details, but you will be aware of it. You’re aware of the architectural things that are wrong. You might not spot it straight away, but there’ll be something about it that won’t ring true. It’ll nag your subconscious.

When an actor walks into a set, and they open the drawer. and it’s full of school reports or whatever is the right thing – or it’s the dentist’s office, and they pull out the drawer, and it’s full of dental gear – that’s a grounding moment for the actor. It’s the exact opposite of standing in front of a blue screen and talking about what our hope is. Everything they’re touching helps them play the role they’re playing, and I take that seriously. I give that detail everything I can. I believe it makes a big difference.


On the sets of “Insidious: Out Of The Further”, courtesy of Nick Bassett and Sony Pictures.

Kirill: What was your thinking about the tattoo parlor? What design elements did you want to see there?

Nick: A typical tattoo parlor you would walk by on the street now is a clinical space. They are quite like a barbershop or a dental clinic. I was talking about it with Jacob, and we decided that it would be better to go for a different look. We didn’t want it to be too clinical and too clean. Our movie takes place in Pittsburgh, and I researched some local areas, and we found an old industrial building with a cool exterior. It was also an opportunity to break out of the suburban world that we were in.

For the mirror sequence, we built the wall with the mirror in it, and then cut a hole that matched that removable mirror. Then we duplicated the set in reverse, and we did it in camera for the most part. That took a lot of rehearsing. You’re trying to move quickly and build these sets, and they’re waiting for you to start the rehearsals. The pillow fort was another example of giving the crew a lot of time to get their head around how they’re going to film it. You stop your art department work for a moment, and you let the camera team and the director and the actors figure out what they’re going to do. Then we come back and address the changes that they require.

For the tattoo parlor we wanted a hit of color and a feeling of looseness to its aesthetic, before we’re returning to that suburban setting. Sometimes you want to have more fun. You pick an angle and that’s what we did on that one.

Kirill: The Further is the last big place in this story. How do you know how much is too much, or how little is too little? How do you strike that balance?

Nick: Five movies have been made, and this concept of the Further has been around for a while. Jacob was leading the way on that. One of the things that we talked about early on was about not trying to reinvent that yet. There’s a lot of room to play with that, but we felt in this movie it was good to keep it familiar to people.

One thing that we added was in the bathroom where you pull out and withdraw the camera into this Further space, and we came up with this idea of a textured black. We pulled the walls off the set, extended the walls out, and painted black marks all the way down the walls that had a texture to them. You start to fade it into the wallpaper as an in-camera transition into complete darkness.

Overall, we didn’t want to veer too far off track. We didn’t want it to feel like a different movie. It was carefully considered. There’s a world where you could investigate that more, and I suspect that will happen. But as you’re introducing new characters and new places, it was wise to hold on to a few of the elements from the previous films.


On the sets of “Insidious: Out Of The Further”, courtesy of Nick Bassett and Sony Pictures.

Kirill: Why should people go to the movie theater to watch this production on the biggest screen they can get?

Nick: It’s not my department, but the sound quality of a cinema isn’t something that an average viewer is going to get at home. It’s a much more immersive experience. I saw “Insidious” a few weeks back when it came out, and you see so much visual richness in it, and that is all intended. People watch movies on their cell phones and on airplanes, and that’s about the worst version of watching a movie that you can imagine [laughs]. The cinema is a superior experience.

The other part of it is to go to a theater and hear people react to it. That reaction is what I remember going to the cinema as a kid – and all through my life. It’s infectious. If someone laughs, it will trigger other people to laugh. If someone screams, it will trigger others. Horror is great for that. If you’re in a full cinema and it’s a good horror movie, it’s a moving energy. This is something that people are discovering again. I do believe we’re going through a new version of people falling in love with cinema again. A full cinema is an amazing experience that has such a huge buzz. It’s creating so much energy.


On the set of the pillow fort tunnels of “Insidious: Out Of The Further”, courtesy of Nick Bassett and Sony Pictures.

Kirill: How do you see generative AI today?

Nick: It’s very present. Even if we’re not using it, it’s talked about all the time. I see those conversations continuing for a long time.

As every creative tool, it’s occasionally quite useful. I’m definitely having a play with using it as a creative device. It is allowing me to get my ideas in order in quite a good way. I don’t see it as something that would give me a brilliant idea, but rather something that is a tool for visual enhancements.

We know all of the perils of it, and it’s almost like a cautionary thing we go into. That said, it’s not replacing anyone. I need set designers. I need builders. I welcome their opinions. My use for AI right now is to get my ideas across. If I want to apply different colors to the 3D set drawing, I could spend a long time doing that in Photoshop, or I can ask the AI to do a quick pass for the colors. It’s a useful tool that speeds my process, and things are speeding up already in the art department as I mentioned earlier.

I am slightly fearful of this aspect. I worry that it’s going to put everyone under much more time pressure. Ultimately, it might not be good for us to arrive so quickly at things that look finished. It might feel like great success to present these amazing things, but it can’t come at the expense of skipping steps and not fully figuring out what works and why it works. I really do like to go back to basics and allow my brain to think about it. But I’m always looking for tools to help me speed up my visual communication – so I’m right on the fence with it.

My kids are in creative fields and I worry for them. The current language around AI is so negative. As a young creative person it’s feeling very threatening, and I worry about that. I was lucky that I got to start at the bottom of an industry. I’ve been able to work as a creative person my whole life, and I’ve been able to do it in a slow-paced, methodical way. And now the expectation is that you can be an expert much quicker. I worry that we’re going to speed up and we’re not going to enjoy the learning.

I sit right on the fence with it. I see it as a useful tool now. I see it as a cautionary tale. What I hope is that anyone who’s interested in design or quality will keep learning to question things. Travel as much as you can. See as much as you can. Talk to people as much as you can. Learn and train your brain to see what reality is. It’s an interesting time. We’ve been through interesting times before, and this feels a little more unpredictable.


The final still of the pillow fort tunnels of “Insidious: Out Of The Further”, courtesy of Sony Pictures.

Kirill: What are the key ingredients or maybe the secrets to longevity in your field?

Nick: It needs to click for you that you’re there to tell a story. I don’t think everyone clicks to that straight away. You’re really there to bring this story to life. Once that clicks, it hooks you in and you realize there’s nothing as much fun as that. You’re privileged to be able to do it.

And then you have to figure out a way to survive the ups and downs of the career path and the financial side of it. If you really enjoy and see the potential in that, that does motivate you to have longevity in the industry.

Having done movies and TV shows seen by a lot of people, you wouldn’t want to listen to the critical audience too much [laughs]. You’re on your own journey. I’m trying to learn as much as I can as I go on each job. What have I learned on this one? How can I bring that to the next one? How can I teach or encourage people to do good work?

It’s a rewarding industry. If you think you’re going to be famous and make a lot of money, it’s definitely not the right fit. It can happen, but it happens to very few [laughs]. Those who love storytelling are hooked for life.

Kirill: If you’re randomly switching TV channels, what would be a movie or two that always grab your attention and make you stop flipping?

Nick: When I’m just trying to relax, I’ll always go to comedy movies. Watching high concept superhero movies is too much for me. I work in the industry and I know how hard they are to make. So I go to things that are quite basic. My wife always laughs. She’ll put on a movie and I’ll fall asleep if it’s too much action. But if it’s two people talking and it’s a good drama movie, I can hook into it. The simpler, the better.

I am drawn to ’80s comedies. That’s my default if I want to relax. I don’t watch all the horrors that come out. I work on them, and I don’t watch them, funnily enough. If someone says watch it as a good reference, I’ll dive into it.

I love a Larry David sketch or Seinfeld. That’s me through and through. You look at the set behind them, and it’s the most basic set you could ever imagine. But it’s so clever in my mind because I’m listening to what these people are saying.

Kirill: Of all your professional travel for work in the last couple of years, what was your favorite dish or cuisine?

Nick: Good Japanese is my default. Melbourne has incredible food throughout the whole city. I wish I remembered the name of this great Japanese restaurant down this little alleyway. It was a street vendor and it was the best. It’s great to go to such a place with somebody who you know well, who you work with a lot, who you travel with a lot. You find a good restaurant, and you can chat about your day and also eat this great food. Anyone who’s traveling to Melbourne will be absolutely spoiled for food.

And here I want to thank Nick Bassett for sharing his time with me to talk about the art and craft of production design, and for sharing the supporting materials. I also want to thank Alix Becq-Weinstein for making this interview happen. “Insidious: Out Of The Further” is playing in movie theaters now. Finally, if you want to know more about how films and TV shows are made, click here for additional in-depth interviews in this series.

item.title: Production design of “Fall 2: Deadpoint” – interview with Jacinta Leong
item.dc:creator: Kirill Grouchnikov
item.description: Continuing the ongoing series of interviews with creative artists working on various aspects of movie and TV productions, it is my pleasure to welcome Jacinta Leong. In this interview, she talks the role of production design and the bigger changes in the art department in the last few decades, key ingredients to longevity in the […]
item.content:encoded:
Continuing the ongoing series of interviews with creative artists working on various aspects of movie and TV productions, it is my pleasure to welcome Jacinta Leong. In this interview, she talks the role of production design and the bigger changes in the art department in the last few decades, key ingredients to longevity in the industry, and experiencing stories on the big screen. Between all these and more, Jacinta takes a deeper look into her work on “Fall 2: Deadpoint”.

Kirill: Please tell us about yourself and what drew you into the world of art department and production design.

Jacinta: I am a film production designer. The production designer is responsible for everything that is on the screen that you see during a film, except for costumes and the actors.

I was drawn into this world step by step. When I was twelve, I wanted to be a performer on stage, whether it be with music or acting. Together with my sisters I went to audition for a stage play called “The King and I”. The set designer, Lindy Whistler, was a qualified architect. I was always interested in drawing buildings, and I thought that if I want to turn up to auditions, I could also study architecture to become a set designer and have a couple of options.

When I turned seventeen, I went to the Queensland University of Technology. In my final year there, I found myself being drawn more to film than theatre. My final year thesis was on set design for film and television, because there is such a crossover between architecture and set design. Many of the principles are the same. Most of the set designers for theatre were architects, because often the backdrops were of a city or a street. That’s how I got drawn into it.

After I finished the course, I started sending my CV out to production designers, art directors and studios. Then I was lucky enough to land a job at the movie studios in Queensland. I also wrote to the production designer Henry Bumstead in the ’90s, asking if I could do some work for him. I joined his art department in the States to work as an intern on a film called “The Stars Fell on Henrietta”, and I was totally hooked by then. That was in the early ’90s, and I haven’t stopped since.


Conceptual art (top) and final still (bottom) of ladders and platform on “Fall 2: Deadpoint”, courtesy of Jacinta Leong.

Kirill: Looking at these 30 years in the industry, what are the bigger changes in how these stories are made from the perspective of the art department?

Jacinta: From the perspective of production design, the principles of designing have not changed. It’s more about the process of creating artwork and drawings to be built, and the way of conveying that to everyone who needs to know what it’s going to look like – be it the director, the cinematographer, or anybody else.

Back in high school I had a subject called geometrical drawing and perspective. We used T-squares, set squares, lead pencils, and erasers. Then, when I was studying for my university degree, I started working in an architectural firm, and they were using AutoCAD. My experience using AutoCAD has been enjoyable, but I’m very glad to have had the lead pencil background.

Going back to film production design, sets were drawn and drafted using pencil and T-square. When I was on “The Stars Fell on Henrietta”, Mr. Bumstead was there with his T-square lead pencils and drawing board. So that’s one change – going from lead pencil drawings to computer drawing, and the 3D aspect of it as well.

The second one is how research has changed with the digital age of the Internet. When I was starting, a production designer would turn up with tubs full of books to bring into the art department. I still do that now. I’ve got some books, and I’ll put post-it notes on and tag pages and add that to the reference packages. But most people do research online.


Design schematics and construction details of ladders and platform on “Fall 2: Deadpoint”, courtesy of Jacinta Leong.

Kirill: Getting to “Fall 2: Deadpoint”, how did it start for you? How did it find its way to you, or maybe how did you find your way to it?

Jacinta: In 2023 I was introduced to the directors, Peter and Michael Spierig. I worked with them on a project which didn’t end up being made. But because we had met on that one, the following year they contacted me to work on “Fall 2: Deadpoint”. It came up quite quickly, and I was only too happy to have the opportunity to work with them on a film that went ahead. I like to travel, so going to Thailand was a great adventure.

Kirill: Starting with the very first set that we see in the movie, which is the house where Shiloh’s sister Jax lives. How did you approach creating that environment?

Jacinta: For economical reasons, if you find a location, that is a good start because it’s already existing. In Thailand, there was a movie house which had been used for another series. It was a two-story interior and exterior, and I would say that the actors did most of the work there to make you believe it’s happening in the USA. You believe they were in the USA because of who they are. We dressed it with pizza boxes, some furniture pieces, and some artwork on the wall. It was quite dimly lit in the background, and that created a morning atmosphere. We didn’t see that much of it. There were scripted items like the table in the kitchen where they’re sitting at, and the lounge room as well.


Building the High Spirits tourist bar on “Fall 2: Deadpoint”, courtesy of Jacinta Leong.

Kirill: Then they move to the tourist camp when they get to Thailand. Was that something that existed or was that something that you built?

Jacinta: We built that from scratch. Jax and Luce appear when they walk through some jungle-ish environment, and they hear music, and then they see this bar for tourists who want to climb Mount Kwan. It didn’t exist. We built that from scratch on a plot of land near a lake within a national park. It was the perfect setting.

One of the design elements was to make use of that lake and have 360-degree views around. Then you have a locker space for them to get their harnesses. And then you have the lodge that you see them in, and we built that in another area of the park. I’m sure the locations team were looking for an isolated bar, but you wouldn’t find something that would be suitable for these backpackers and tourists with the flexibility to shoot it in day and night with a film crew. That’s how we ended up building the set to get the shots that we wanted.

Kirill: When they get to the set of the fictitious Mount Kwan, where was that shot, what existed there, and what did you add?

Jacinta: Peter and Michael wanted the height for the planks because we wanted to look up to them in their perilous positions. You can only go so high before it becomes quite time-consuming to shoot. So we set planks at a maximum of about six meters off the ground, because the camera cranes could only reach so far. That was the best way to achieve those shots.

What existed in the first place was a quarry about 2.5 hours drive from Bangkok. We had a rock climbing expert assess the quarry walls for safety and strength. Originally we thought that we may have to put planks up not into the wall, but actually support them from the ground with scaffolding – and then we’d have to have VFX erase those supports digitally. But thankfully, after the testing it was found that we would drill into those rock faces safely and place the planks on the brackets that we put in.


Conceptual art (top) and final still (bottom) of Devil’s Elbow on “Fall 2: Deadpoint”, courtesy of Jacinta Leong.

Kirill: Without too many spoilers beyond the movie trailer, the story spends a lot of time in the Devil’s Elbow. What was the setup you envisioned for building the structure there and how much work went into it?

Jacinta: The vision was to have the two climbers stranded at an extreme height. And we wanted the camera to shoot it in a way that places the audiences directly into that experience through immersive filmmaking.

The script called for it to have a huge, breathtaking view the first time they see it. We needed to have them at that height and at that sharp angle, and that feature didn’t exist at the quarry. That’s why we built it. There’s so much other action there that demanded a set build as well. You see it in the trailers when they’re hanging with their arms from those rungs, or they’re stepping and standing on them.

It was built using scaffolding and polystyrene in that initial sharp arrowhead shape. It was built in a workshop in a flat area of ground where they had room, and then it was transported to site and assembled using a crane.


Design schematics of Devil’s Elbow on “Fall 2: Deadpoint”, courtesy of Jacinta Leong.

Kirill: The last big piece is the sky bridge closer to the end of the movie. How much of it is real, and how much is the visual effects or set extensions?

Jacinta: The length of the bridge, the rock face that they start in to get to that bridge, and the platform at the end – they were all real. As Michael and Peter were determined to use the natural light and landscape of that area in Thailand, it was built at that same quarry with the sun setting on that side. It was engineered as well. It had to be safe for three actors to walk across – plus camera crew, makeup, stunts – all on that platform.

We had several versions of that bridge. At one point it was a rigid timber bridge to be in keeping with the planks. We were looking at so many bridges that are high up around the world. And then one of the things Michael said was that it could be a tight rope. I looked at steel wire cables together with planks to have it consistent with that world. That was a different kind of plank. It was one that would move and sway. It was broken down and dilapidated. And, again, we were pushing that fear and making it feel that you wouldn’t step on it.


Building process of Devil’s Elbow on “Fall 2: Deadpoint”, courtesy of Jacinta Leong.

Kirill: Do you want people to go and see it on the biggest screen possible? Do you want people to go and see it in the movie theater?

Jacinta: I would love the audience to go and see “Fall 2: Deadpoint” in the movie theater. The experience is worlds apart from watching it on TV at home. It’ll be a more immersive experience, and the sound will really place you there as well. The scenery in Thailand deserves the big screen. I hope the audience enjoys having their buttons pushed.

Kirill: What are the key ingredients to longevity in your field?

Jacinta: The key to longevity in this field is that you have to really enjoy it. I don’t know if it’s talent, skill, or a willingness to be involved. But you really must want to be working on films to have that longevity.


Before and after the completed construction of Devil’s Elbow on “Fall 2: Deadpoint”, courtesy of Jacinta Leong.

Kirill: What was your favorite dish or food that you had in Thailand while you were working on this movie?

Jacinta: I’m from Australia, and Thai cuisine has a lot of spicy food. There were a couple of occasions I would line up to the food that they had, and then the person in control of the food would say “Oh, put this spicy dish away, have that plain rice over there” [laughs]. I’m going to say it was vegetarian Thai fried rice.


Constructed set (top) and final still (bottom) of walking planks on “Fall 2: Deadpoint”, courtesy of Jacinta Leong.


Constructed set (top) and final still (bottom) of the bridge to peak of Mount Kwan on “Fall 2: Deadpoint”, courtesy of Jacinta Leong.


Building process of the aircraft cabin on “Fall 2: Deadpoint”, courtesy of Jacinta Leong.

And here I’d to thank Jacinta Leong for sharing her time with me to talk about the art and craft of production design, and for sharing the supporting materials. I also want to thank Jackson Vickery for making this interview happen. “Fall 2: Deadpoint” is playing in theaters now. Finally, if you want to know more about how films and TV shows are made, click here for additional in-depth interviews in this series.

Among the many memorable sets on “Stranger Things”, one stood out in particular during the show’s final season – Holly Wheeler’s bedroom. In our earlier interview, the show’s set decorator Jess Royal says this:

You see this happy bright colorful room, and then all of a sudden a monster is coming through the ceiling and trying to steal her. It’s that fun “Stranger Things” contrast.

item.content:encoded:
Continuing the ongoing series of interviews with creative artists working on various aspects of movie and episodic productions, it is my pleasure to welcome Jeanie Bacharach. Jeanie is a triple Emmy Award winner for her work on “The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel” and “The Bear”, and among her many other credits are “Ally McBeal”, “The Dropout”, “Black Mirror”, “Lucky”, “Brothers & Sisters” and “Nashville”. In this interview, Julie takes a deep dive into her Emmy-nominated work on the second season of “Beef”.

Kirill: Please tell us about yourself and the path that took you to where you are today.

Jeanie: I started out as an actress, very briefly, in New York. Then I was a reader for auditions, and it opened me up to the other side of the industry and casting. I found that quite fascinating, and still creative to this day. That was my start in casting in New York where I worked primarily in theater. Later on my husband and I moved out here to Los Angeles, and made my way mostly in television. That’s been the main focus of my casting career.

Kirill: What are the bigger misunderstandings or misconceptions about the role of the casting director, and what goes into it?

Jeanie: People don’t quite understand what we’re doing behind the scenes. So much of it is about personal taste, and what you respond to in an actor and in their work. The wonderful thing about it is it’s subjective. What I might respond to in an actor, someone else might not, and vice versa. I try to tell young actors to always keep that in mind. Whatever feedback you’re getting is coming from one person’s experience or perception.

Taste is a key point. People don’t realize that there’s a collaborative aspect of it. We are there at the very beginning, often before maybe even a director is on. We’re trying to take the writer’s vision and bring it to life. But part of our job is to try to expand whatever that idea may be. When they were writing it, they may have thought a specific way. But what’s so fun and maybe not as understood about what we do is that we then try to take that and stretch it as much as we can while still serving the piece and the character. You can’t become arbitrary and have it at the detriment of the story you’re telling.

Then, you’re working behind the scenes to set actors up to succeed as best possible. Sometimes that means finding a piece of film on them that other people may not have seen that can help a director or writer to see their work in a different light.

It’s so collaborative, and you’re there from the beginning. One way to see it is that you give birth to the project, and then it’s up to the rest of the creative team to go from there.


(L to R) Charles Melton as Austin Davis, Cailee Spaeny as Ashley Miller, Carey Mulligan as Lindsay Crane-Martin, Oscar Isaac as Josh Martin in episode 202 of Beef. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: Did it feel that the recognition of your craft at the Oscars was overdue?

Jeanie: Certainly, as every other part of the creative process has been recognized up to this point. It was way overdue and very exciting. I don’t quite understand what took so long, but I’m so glad we’re there.

Kirill: What are the bigger differences between the feature film world and the episodic productions, and why do you mostly stay in the episodic world?

Jeanie: When I first started in television, there wasn’t as much streaming and cable. It was pretty much all network TV. As streaming and cable came into being. and there started to be the crossover of feature people – directors and writers and actors – into television and back and forth, the differences starting getting smaller.

The biggest difference is we have to work much faster in television than in feature films, because the schedule is so different. Once you get into casting a series, you have anywhere from eight to ten days to cast an episode, whereas in feature films you generally have months of preparation.
Another thing about casting in television is that since you don’t have that much time, you need to know that actors are going to be able to deliver in the moment. And yet another one is that no matter if you’re casting for a long term series or for a limited one, it can be eight or ten or twelve hours of screen time. You need to find actors that people are going to invest in and want to watch over a period of time. On a feature film you’re holding a much bigger screen, but for a relatively shorter period of time.

You’re looking at a longer period of time when you are casting for a series. You have a deeper development of the character in a series. A feature film may cover a large period of time or a shorter period of time, but in television, more often than not, where your character starts and where it ends can be very different. You need to know that the actor can carry all of those beats and story points over multiple episodes and/or seasons.


(L to R) Seoyeon Jang as Eunice, Charles Melton as Austin Davis, Cailee Spaeny as Ashley Miller in episode 203 of Beef. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: Getting to “Beef”, how did it start for you?

Jeanie: Sonny [Lee Sun Jin, the creator of the show] reached out to me and wanted to know if I would be interested in talking about Season Two – to which I said “Yes, of course, I’m there. Just tell me where to show up” [laughs]. We had an initial meeting and hit it off from the beginning. We started talking about his ideas for the story for Season Two in that meeting.

Kirill: What drew you in the most on this show?

Jeanie: The tone on the show is so interesting. You have these heightened situations while still remaining grounded, real, and relatable. The challenge of walking that line for me is so interesting. He had also talked about the emotional depth that the characters were going to need to do this Season Two, and that was interesting to me as well.

Kirill: How much time did you spend on the show?

Jeanie: Several months between before they started filming through to when they finished filming.

Kirill: Who were your primary collaborators on it?

Jeanie: Sonny for sure was who I worked with most closely. I also worked with my partners over at A24 and Netflix, but in terms of exploration of the characters and the day-to-day collaboration, it was with Sonny.


(L to R) William Fichtner as Troy, Oscar Isaac as Josh Martin, Benny Blanco as self, Baron Davis as self in episode 202 of Beef.  Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: How do you usually start this? Do you start with the primary characters and then go for the supporting cast?

Jeanie: In this case, yes. We started with our regulars, and then built out from there with the larger roles.

When I started on it, we didn’t have all the scripts. A lot of it was conversations with Sonny as he was thinking about these characters and where they might go. That’s where the collaboration is also so wonderful. He has maybe an idea of a character, and then as I’m suggesting actors or as we talk about it, it may move in a slightly different direction. Or an actor may make him think of the character in a different way than he had originally thought. Or I may suggest an actor to him, and he will say that while it works for this particular part of the story, this is where I’m thinking about going with it, and I’m not sure that that actor serves that purpose. There’s so much give and take. It’s a trust that starts to build between us where both of us can push each other to think a little more outside the box.

Kirill: What are your thoughts on typecasting? How difficult is it for everybody involved to not fall into that trap?

Jeanie: It goes back again to the trust element. When you have people you’re working with that you trust and they trust you, that allows you to think outside the box and turn an expectation of a role on its head. You can cast somebody who comes with a certain preconceived idea, and you then take the audience in that direction with that actor cast in a stereotypical way – and then you turn it in a way that the audience doesn’t expect.

Sometimes casting to type that way can be good if you want to set people up on an expectation and then pull the rug out from underneath them. And sometimes you may see the actor in this stereotypical way, but you’ve also seen them do other things. I started in theater, and that’s a big part of it for me. I saw actors do so many different things. I came up watching people who trained and studied their craft. They know how to play drama, they know how to play comedy, they can do heightened, they can do naturalistic. From that basis, I try to look at actors as a whole and not as a stereotype of what they may be best known for.

It’s so hard for actors. If you’re lucky enough to land on a TV series that runs for a long time, you become known as that character. It’s great because you’ve made a living, but then you have to spend the rest of your career convincing people that you can do other things. We’re moving so quickly, and I have to remind myself that it’s too easy to say that a certain actor is not right because you think of them a certain way. Part of your job as a casting director is to try to know people’s body of work as broadly as possible, and not just the way most people know them. Part of our job is to go the extra mile and look at actors’ work that may not be as well known.


(L to R) Song Kang-ho as Dr. Kim, Youn Yuh-jung as Chairwoman Park in episode 203 of Beef. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: Going back to the show and the South Korean part of it, is it becoming easier in this global world to keep track of the international talent and find the right people?

Jeanie: For sure. You can get on a Zoom call with an actor in another part of the world. Or you can have them make a tape and have it arrive in your email box 10 minutes later. It’s completely changed it. It’s opened up the world immensely. There’s also a tremendous amount of international television and films now available, and that has completely changed the game as well.

Kirill: You worked on “Ally McBeal” in the late ’90s, and that was absolutely my favorite show back then. Do you feel that it’s easier, if you will, to get the big name actors to do episodic productions these days compared to how it was back then?

Jeanie: Absolutely, and that is also tied to the writers and the directors who have been attracted to television. Actors are looking for good stories and good characters to play.

Going back to what I said before, if you’re a feature actor, the idea of being able to explore a character over ten hours of episodic versus two hours of a film can be exciting. If you’re working with cable or streaming, and you’re doing 10-12 episodes, you then have the whole other half of your year to do a film. When it was back in the network TV broadcast world, you were doing 22 episodes a season, and it didn’t leave much time to do anything else.


(L to R) Cailee Spaeny as Ashley Miller, Oscar Isaac as Josh Martin in episode 202 of Beef. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: Do you want to have exceptional actors as individuals or an exceptional cast?

Jeanie: To me it’s the whole which is so important. I understand a studio and a network’s desire to have recognized names in significant roles. There’s so much product out there and you’re trying to get eyeballs to your show. So there is that desire to have somebody who can get on a talk show or somebody who has a following already.

But to me, if they don’t fit in the world and they don’t work together with the rest of the cast, it doesn’t matter how famous they may be. It has to work. People have to come back to the show. They might come to the show initially because of some name recognition of a famous actor in it. But you need them to come back, and keep watching. That’s why to me, it’s about the ensemble as a whole and not just that particular actor.

Kirill: Maybe, and correct me if I’m wrong, there’s also less appetite from the studios to bet on a completely unknown cast and give that new show a couple of years to find its legs. Maybe now it’s more about hitting it straight out the gate.

Jeanie: It depends on how big the show is. If it’s an extremely expensive show to make, there’s more pressure to have known entities in it. But there’s so many successful shows that did not have known actors before they were in the show. It really depends upon the project itself and the platform. There are places that are willing to take more chances than perhaps some others. I do think it mostly depends on the size of the show. And I actually think there is more openness than there used to be.

Kirill: Going back to “Beef” for my last question on the show. You start working on it so early in its development, and then it goes to shooting, and then to editing, and then the network decides when to air it. And then you sit down and watch it. How does it feel to go back to that story after all these long months that you’ve been away from it, so to speak?

Jeanie: It’s great. I have to watch it a couple times. The first time I might be looking at the actors that we took a chance on and I’m a little anxious as to how they did. Then the second time, I’m really in it.

Sometimes there’s a role that took a long time to cast, and you read the same scene over and over and over during the auditions, and then you finally see it, and it’s a little bit triggering. I remember the process the first time I’m watching [laughs]. It’s always exciting to see it all come together. I’m there from the very beginning. Then you have production design, costume design, makeup, props and editing bringing the rest of the piece together.


(L to R) Cailee Spaeny as Ashley Miller, Carey Mulligan as Lindsay Crane-Martin in episode 206 of Beef. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: Some people see generative AI as an existential threat to creativity, and some see it as yet another tool to adopt and adapt and to add to their arsenal. Where do you find yourself these days?

Jeanie: I would say the former. Going back to what I was saying earlier about what casting is. It’s about personal taste. It’s about being able to see something in an actor’s audition performance. It might not be exactly right, but you see something there, and you work with it.

If we lose our humanity, especially in casting, we’re really lost. So much of it is about being able to work with an actor and to see something in there, even if they didn’t fully land it, and helping them to find it. There’s so much vulnerability that is required from an actor. The further removed we come to be from that process, the more we’re going to lose in the storytelling and our ability as an audience to connect and to see ourselves in those characters and in those performances.

Kirill: What are the key ingredients to longevity in your industry?

Jeanie: From an acting perspective, it’s about training and understanding that it’s a craft, and not just about being discovered on TikTok or having a certain look.

You need adaptability, humanity, and compassion for the people you’re working with. You need respect for the people you’re working with. You need a collaborative spirit. And you need just the right amount of ego to fight for what you feel strongly about. And you also need to understand that you’re part of a whole, and that sometimes maybe you’re not seeing the whole picture. Sometimes you’re digging in your heels for your own ego or whatever it might be – and not hearing what the director or the writer is saying isn’t working from your perspective.

You need to work well with others, and walk the right line of personal investment and passion without letting it be absolutely everything in your life. You need to have a balance in your life.

Kirill: Is there a piece of advice you would want to give to your younger self if you could jump back in time to the late ’90s?

Jeanie: Trust the process. Trust the journey. Stay true to your beliefs, and what’s important to you and your creative soul. Trust that eventually you’ll find the people who understand that and see that. And enjoy the ride.

Kirill: Out of all the travels you had for work over your career so far, what was the place that had the best food?

Jeanie: I had some amazing meals in Chicago working on “The Bear”. There were a couple different restaurants there that I only would have known about from working on the show and introductions that were made from people working on the show. That made the meals all the more special.


(L to R) Charles Melton as Austin Davis, Cailee Spaeny as Ashley Miller, Carey Mulligan as Lindsay Crane-Martin in episode 208 of Beef. Cr. Courtesy of Netflix.

And here I want to thank Jeanie Bacharach for sharing her time with me to talk about the art and craft of casting. I also want to thank Kristy Chan for making this interview happen. “Beef” is streaming on Netflix. Finally, if you want to know more about how films and TV shows are made, click here for additional in-depth interviews in this series.

item.content:encoded:
Continuing the ongoing series of interviews with creative artists working on various aspects of movie and episodic productions, it is my pleasure to welcome Olga Mill. In this interview, she talks about her journey into the world of costume design, key ingredients to longevity in the industry, and her thoughts on generative AI. Between all these and more, Olga dives deep into her Emmy-nominated work on the second season of “Beef”.


Olga Mill on the sets of “Beef”.

Kirill: Please tell us about yourself and the path that took you to where you are today.

Olga: I knew I wanted to do what I do today pretty early on. My family moved to New York from the Ukraine when I was five. They would take us to the theater all the time, and I also went into community theater acting programs. Later on I went to a performing arts high school in New York. The acting part of it didn’t resonate with me, but I did like the parts about making your own sets and costumes.

I remember walking home from school one day and thinking that I could be a costume designer. The more I thought about it, the more it looked like it would let me out of some of the acting stuff that didn’t resonate, and also that it appealed to a nerdier research part of myself. It also felt more practical in a way. That’s when my path started, back in high school.

It took a long time to feel confident enough to want to be in the designer role. In the film industry, if your family’s not in it, it can feel so out of reach. So at first I was thinking that I would be happy if I could just work in a costume shop. And then I wanted to be an assistant. And only when I went to graduate school at NYU that I felt ready to go for the head of department role.


Costume design of “Beef” by Olga Mill. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: What are the misconceptions or misunderstandings about what costume design is?

Olga: The first one is that a lot of people assume that I know how to sew. It’s really important to understand the construction and design because I’m talking to tailors. But left to my own devices, it’s a skill that I don’t have. I respect it a lot, but I certainly wouldn’t be able to do it myself.

The second misconception is putting costume design in with fashion. Fashion is its own lane that I have so much respect for, but that’s not where the meat of my knowledge is. As a costume designer, you are driven by the script and the characters and not the aesthetics of fashion. I don’t mean to downplay fashion, but these are two independent avenues that often get intertwined. They are different skill sets.

Kirill: Getting to “Beef”, how did you find your way to it, or perhaps how did it find its way to you?

Olga: I feel that we met each other halfway. I was a big fan of season one, and I had worked with the production designer Grace Yun several times in the past. I got the script for the second season through my agent, and I don’t know if it was through Grace or through my past work with A24.

I met Sonny [Lee Sun Jin, the creator of the show] for a coffee, and he laid out his thoughts for season two. It’s an anthology series, and it was interesting for me because you can start from scratch with new characters. I put together some visuals and sent him, and then we went from there.


Costume sketches for “Beef”, courtesy of Olga Mill and Netflix. Left to right – Ashley, Austin, Ashley.

Kirill: What is the most interesting part of this season for you?

Olga: I’m 41 years old, and I’m a part of the millennial generation. It feels that my generation is culturally at the part of the curve where enough time has passed from your twenties and certain trends when you can look back and start to see the things that were popular in a more objective way. You need a little bit of distance, maybe 10-15 years [laughs] to be able to reflect on it.

The show deals so much with how generations are interacting with each other, and it was the chance to look at millennial culture in an anthropological way for the first time. I didn’t do that before, and it was quite humbling at times.


Costume sketches for “Beef”, courtesy of Olga Mill and Netflix. Left to right – Joshua, Chairwoman Park, Lindsay.

Kirill: There’s generational divide, cultural divide, class divide and others in the show. How did you approach this? How wide of a canvas did it give you to explore in your department?

Olga: Even though it takes place in the modern day, I do modern day projects the same way as if I’m doing a period film. It’s a different part of society for me. I didn’t grow up going to country clubs, so that was new.

We spent a lot of time at the Montecito Country Club. We spent time in Ojai. Bailey Gardner who was the assistant costume designer and I, together with Grace and Kellie Jo Tinney the set decorator would go to both those towns, have lunch and look around. The other place where I do a lot of research is Instagram. It’s amazing. You think about the characters of Josh and Lindsay and Ashley and Austin – they would be posting stuff online. So I spent a lot of time trying to find real accounts that I thought had elements that spoke to the characters. Sonny, Grace, James Laxton the cinematographer and I would send them back and forth to each other.

It was trying to find real people who lived in Ojai or who were in Montecito. It’s a costume designer’s dream. They post their outfit of the day. They post the brands where they shop. I’m researching it like I’m researching the 1500s in England., to get a sense of where these people shop, and what’s important to them.


Costume design of “Beef” by Olga Mill. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: How did you approach the differences in culture, traditions and environment for the South Korean characters?

Olga: Our window into Korea is very specifically through the lens of Chairwoman Park, who is not just Korean, but super ultra-wealthy Korea. There’s the scene where she comes in and looks at the room that Lindsay designed at the country club. Grace did such a beautiful job with that room. It’s not garish, but it’s not quite a room that amazes you. It doesn’t make you want to be in that space.

Everything about the Korean aesthetic that we were trying to represent was in opposition of what the style of that room is. It is more modern. It is more sleek. The term “quiet luxury” is overplayed, but it is there. Lindsay’s design is stuff on stuff on stuff. And the Korean aesthetic here is simpler and more refined.

Originally we looked at examples of real Korean ultra-wealthy women in that age group, and it’s a cashmere world. We did veer from that with Chairwoman Park, giving her the leather jacket. She represents modernity, but there’s elements that are unexpected to her as well. I wouldn’t say that she is the typical Korean woman of that age. There is a certain worldliness to her. But overall, just in opposition to Lindsay’s aesthetic, that was a good guiding light.


Costume design of “Beef” by Olga Mill. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: One of the parts of the storyline that I liked was how the four main characters try to blend in in an environment that is a completely different tax bracket, an environment that has a completely different set of financial means. Joshua and Lindsay want to be seen as almost equals, but they’re not quite there with the money. And the young couple has their own aspirations, especially Ashley.

Olga: The term “hyper assimiliation” came up quite frequently. It is almost like an immigrant experience, but through class instead of countries. Take Josh for example. The way I thought of him and talked to Oscar Isaac about him is how he walks through the club. He’s clocking how people are dressed. He has to be really aware of it, and then constantly trying to mimic it – again for his own ego – to feel like he’s an equal at the club.

But I also think it’s in service to the members too. This is what I noticed in the spaces of these country clubs. Part of what the members are paying for is to feel like they’re not interacting with employees. There’s something about interacting with somebody who you know is paid to be there that doesn’t feel as good. What feels really good is when you’re interacting with somebody who you don’t feel that class divide. They know your name. They know what you like to drink. Ultimately, it’s because you don’t want to feel guilty for having more than somebody else. So it’s important for Josh to look like the club members because it feels better for everybody.


Costume design of “Beef” by Olga Mill. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: As these main characters move up and down the class hierarchy, if you will, throughout the show’s storyline, what changes did you want to make in their costumes?

Olga: I thought about it more like mirroring each other. When Ashley becomes jealous of Eunice, she starts to dress like her. Her shirts become a little bit more silky. She starts to mimic her professional style. Then when they go to Korea and she’s with Lindsay, she’s in that dress that they’re in at the clinic which is trying to mimic this Montecito prairie aesthetic. And then at the very end when she takes over Josh’s position, she’s in a green suit the way that Josh started the show in. The way I was thinking about it was who are you trying to reflect – or whose skin do you want to put on – and not up and down.

When we first meet Austin, he’s a trainer, but we intentionally made him not wear any athletic fabrics. Everything is cotton, sun washed, and casual. And then, as he starts moving up in the club, he starts wearing moisture wicking official workout fabric.

At any given moment in the season, it was about who you are reflecting and whose life you want.


Costume design of “Beef” by Olga Mill. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: Is there such a thing as your favorite character in this season to work with?

Olga: On a TV show the picture is so much bigger, and you have so much more space with these characters. So they all come in and out of favor, so to speak.

I thought Chairwoman Park was a very interesting character to design. Sometimes characters surprise me. You think this is what they’re going to look like. You do the research, you talk about it with the director, you make the boards, you show the pictures. And it’s not until you’re in a room with somebody until you realize that it’s something different. Her character was the one that I found the most surprising where we landed. In retrospect, it has a softer place in my heart because the process was the most unexpected.


Costume sketches for “Beef”, courtesy of Olga Mill and Netflix.

Kirill: Was there a color that you wanted to particularly emphasize, and was there a color that you didn’t want to use at all?

Olga: Not for the whole show. We did have an intentional map or color theory between Grace, James and I, which was thinking about each couple as a different season.

Color-wise, Lindsay and Josh are very autumnal. It’s purples, oranges, greens, brown, thinking of their relationship is like autumn. Things are drying up and kind of dying. In contrast, Ashley and Austin are spring. It’s all pastels and a spring palette. And then Chairwoman Park is winter. It’s icy grays and light blues. And then the club was an endless summer. That’s where the greens and yellows come in. That was a really helpful way to work to have this color plan that you’re all standing under. Then when you’re making tiny decisions – like what sock should Ashley be in – it comes to which sock feels the most like spring. You give yourself a little map for when you get lost.


Costume design of “Beef” by Olga Mill. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: How do you see AI generative AI today?

Olga: If I’m being really honest, I feel that I don’t know enough about it to have a dogmatic point of view on it. Like with most things in history and in life, it’s not so much what the tool is – it’s what the intention behind it is. Anything can be used productively and anything can be used destructively. I hope it makes most of people’s lives more comfortable, but I don’t know if that’s the case.

It’s easier for me to understand how it makes me personally feel. It is the first time that I feel a sense of aging. You feel that it’s almost a glacier that’s moving and turning – in a zoomed out way of time and technology. I do remember the time before we had the Internet, but I was also young enough that it felt like second nature for it to be around. It wasn’t a concept I had to wrap my mind around. And this feels like the first innovation that makes me feel old, because it feels like something that’s moving. It’s something that I’m not standing on, you know?


Costume design of “Beef” by Olga Mill. Courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: What are the key ingredients to longevity in this field?

Olga: It’s being a person that people want to be in a room and have a conversation with, whether that’s the director, the actors, or the producer who’s talking to you about the budget. It’s being somebody who people want to figure out problems with. Nothing is going to go as planned on any project you’re going to make. There’s going to be problems. It’s like a marriage. Who do you want to sit across the table with and figure out a problem with?

Another part of it is a real privilege, which is having the financial flexibility to be able to pick and choose which projects you want to do. It’s a recurring theme for people that are able to do it for a long time. If you can keep your overhead life expenses smaller so that you don’t have to take every project that comes up, that you can be intentional about which projects you want to take, that is super valuable as a designer.

Kirill: What was your favorite dish that you had while working on the show in South Korea?

Olga: There was this little dumpling shop right next to our office in Seoul, run by an older Korean lady making dumpling soup. It only had a few things on the menu, nothing fancy. Our first day at the office our translator took me there, and that was my favorite spot. It was delicious.


Costume design of “Beef” by Olga Mill. Courtesy of Netflix.

And here I want to thank Olga Mill for sharing her time with me to talk about the art and craft of costume design, and for sharing the supporting materials. I also want to thank Marilyn Lintel for making this interview happen. “Beef” is streaming on Netflix. Finally, if you want to know more about how films and TV shows are made, click here for additional in-depth interviews in this series.
