item.content:encoded:
Continuing the ongoing series of interviews with creative artists working on various aspects of movie and TV productions, it is my pleasure to welcome Jess Royal. In this interview, she talks the role of set decoration and the bigger changes in her department in the last decade, key ingredients to longevity in the industry, and her thoughts on generative AI. Between all these and more, Jess takes a deep dive into her Emmy-nominated work on “Stranger Things”, from its early days to the final season.

Kirill: Please tell us about yourself and the path that took you to where you are today.

Jess: I’m Jess Royal. I’m a set decorator and I did all five seasons of “Stranger Things”. My background is in law. I went to law school and practiced criminal defense. I had some faith going into it that some people are wrongly accused or overcharged, but in my case, our clients were very much guilty [laughs]. The thought of doing that for the rest of my life was quite daunting, and I felt an urge to do something creative.

I didn’t know what that was going to be right away. I found my way into film based on watching background interviews of production designers and set decorators who did period sets on movies and TV shows. I love history, and that was the best possible merge of both worlds. Fortunately, I met a production designer on an elevator, and I would not let go until I got what I wanted, and here I am now.

Kirill: What are the misconceptions or maybe misunderstandings about your role?

Jess: My mom still calls me a set designer, because that’s what the words make sense in her brain, even though a set designer is more of a draftsman who draws up the plans. Perhaps people draw a connection to interior designers that do a full design. People hear set decoration, and think about curtains or sofas or the frilly little details at the end.

The best thing about my job is doing junkyards and huge equipment. It’s doing a landscape that I can build from scratch – exteriors and interiors. It can be drapery, but it’s also every stack of newspaper or a collection of tchotchkes. You can build a backstory of where someone’s been in their life, what they’ve collected, what’s important to them.

I feel like “decoration” is the wrong word. It’s designing a whole world and a whole backstory for a character or a town, using objects, exterior and interior.


Left to right – production designer Chris Trujillo, set decorator Jess Royal, and art director Sean Brennan on the Mayor Cline’s bedroom set of “Stranger Things”. Courtesy of Jess Royal and Netflix.

Kirill: What would be the bigger change that happened in your part of the world, comparing today vs when you were starting out?

Jess: Before, we didn’t have the option to fix things in post with VFX. You had to think about everything – something like covering a transformer on a telephone pole half a mile down the road that someone would see that’s not period. Now we make a note for VFX. Sometimes it’s handy, but I also miss thinking about everything in 360. On “Stranger Things” we started with Schindler boxes to do playback on older TVs to prevent flicker on camera, and now everyone is using green screens to put it in post. It’s mostly about technology and VFX.

Kirill: Getting to “Stranger Things”, how did it start for you, and what stood out in those early days?

Jess: I worked with the production designer Chris Trujillo for a few years before the show on smaller indie movies, and we kept saying that one day we’re going to get a show or a movie that everyone’s going to watch, and we’ll really have made it in the world.

I was in Los Angeles on a vacation, about to get on a plane, and he texted that he was sending a script with a good potential for me to read and to see what I think. Originally it was called “Montauk” and that’s where we were supposed to shoot it. I read the script on the plane, and I thought that it could be so amazing. One thing led to another, and we were scouting in Wilmington for Montauk, and eventually they said that maybe we can look in Atlanta and change the setting of the show. No matter what though, I felt that it had great potential.

It felt very small at the beginning. Netflix was hesitant to give us money to do everything we wanted to do, but then it came out, and it was amazing. It felt that our lives changed, as everyone watched it within 48 hours. It was cool to grow up in those early months of the first season or two.


Jess Royal on the sets of “Stranger Things”. Courtesy of Jess Royal and Netflix.

Kirill: Was it that immediate for you after the first season dropped?

Jess: The release premiere in LA was somewhere outside of West Hollywood. I remember we were sitting on folding chairs, and how small it still felt. But it caught on so fast. I went straight from LA to a wedding in Massachusetts, and by the time I got to Massachusetts a day or two later, my brother had watched it, my mom had watched it, people at the wedding had watched it. Everyone was talking about it, or at least the people I was surrounded with, whether they were watching it for my sake or not. It felt like it was blowing up right away.

I’d already started scouting for “Ozark” at that time. My original film job was the location scout and then I became a decorator, so on some of those earlier shows I would scout and then I’d start prepping decorating. “Ozark” was fun to scout for and I was excited about doing it, and then at some point a few weeks in “Stranger Things” was immediately picked up for season two. So I had to leave “Ozark” a little bit early. I was bummed about that, but I think I made the right choice to stick with “Stranger Things” and what we had built. Merchandise and various experiences came later, but everyone hearing about the show was pretty immediate.


On the sets of the Byers’ living room of “Stranger Things”. Courtesy of Jess Royal and Netflix.

Kirill: Looking back at these 10 years and the entire story arc, why did people connect so much with this show?

Jess: It’s a multi-generational show. One of my best friends is about the age of Jonathan in the show, and he was a photographer in high school and later went to college at Pratt for photography. People his age identify with all the music of the era. They were kids in high school right at that same time. He immediately loved it, and I ended up using his photography as Jonathan’s background photography in the dark room and bedroom.

People his age who now have kids who are around the younger kids’ age in the show can watch it together as family. It transcends generations. It also lends itself well to having a pop culture – the music, the D&D aspect for all the nerds out there who love it. This game has been going strong since the ’80s, and there’s so many generations that can enjoy that aspect. You cheer for these kids and it doesn’t matter how old you are. You want to see them beat the dark forces and stay friends. Watching them grow up has been a delightful thing for a lot of people who have grown up with these kids as the show has gone on.


On the sets of “Stranger Things”. Courtesy of Jess Royal and Netflix.

Kirill: Looking at all the seasons, as it kept on expanding to the mall and the Russian subterranean base, and going to Lithuania for the Russian prison, and so much in the Upside Down – how was it to see the increased scope of your work, and how did you approach it?

Jess: It’s not just “Stranger Things”, but also film in general. There’s been a little bit of a turn in the industry, and we felt it on season five. Studios are pulling back a little bit as far as some of the money they’d spent on productions.

I would have told you that there’s no way that we could do season three for less money or with less people than we have now. But as that constrained slowly, we did season five with a little bit less resources, at least for our department. You grow with what you have. You are challenged, and you know how to do that the next time. It comes with experience. I don’t know if I could have gotten that much experience out of 10 years of doing anything else. “Stranger Things” kept on ramping up every season, and the expectations got higher and higher.

Season three was probably the hardest that we did. We built the entire mall from the ground up. Everything was dressed. All the stores had everything in them. And at the same time I’m planning the carnival. It was a multi-million dollar expenditure to get all the rides, to get all the original incandescent lighting and other things. And then season four got even bigger because we’re on different continents. If anything, season five spends a lot of time in the Upside Down, so there’s less things to do for set decoration. You take it as it comes, and if it doesn’t kill you, it makes you stronger.


Set decoration of “Stranger Things” by Jess Royal, courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: How disruptive was Covid for your department?

Jess: Everyone shut down, so it was less disruptive than the writer’s strike was for season five. We still had some people working and building, but set decoration was out of the loop for a while. We came back to all these sets that were built, and a lot of decisions had to be made really fast to get them dressed so we could start shooting right away.

I was working from home, keeping in touch with some friends in Russia who supplied us with computers and some other things. They were still shipping technology back to the US that I was gathering. That way, when we got back in from Covid, I was ready to hit the ground running. We started going back to Lithuania to scout. When everyone stops at the same time, it doesn’t feel as oppressive. The biggest problem there was just the kids looked so much older after we came back [laughs].


Jess Royal’s dog on the set of Holly’s room on “Stranger Things”. Courtesy of Jess Royal and Netflix.

Kirill: What are your personal highlights of the fifth season of the show?

Jess: I think the production designer and art director and I all agree that the radio station was one of our crowning achievements for the whole show. It brought in so many elements. We built the exterior fully around the Palmetta area in Georgia, and the residents that were driving by were not able to figure out what it was. You have all the neon lights, and the start of the tower right there on site. There was so much research around how everything should look like – the transmitter, the copper lines for certain spaces, etc.

It was based on a real radio station in North Carolina that the Duffers grew up nearby that they were always inspired by. Chris had found it in his research on radio stations, so it synced once they saw that in his lookbook. We copied pretty much the whole layout of that station. We ended up going up there, and picking up some of their dead equipment and elements that they had at the actual radio station, and bringing it back to Atlanta. Then we made it fit within the world of “Stranger Things”, adding a livable hangout space with all the records. It was so much fun for me to select all those bumper stickers on the walls.

Then we have Holly’s room. I always loved the floral Marimekko wallpapers that you see in old references and magazines from the late ’70s to early ’80s. It was so exciting to use it there, as it ended up being my dream bedroom that I never had as a kid. It also is such a hard contrast with what happens in that bedroom. You see this happy bright colorful room, and then all of a sudden a monster is coming through the ceiling and trying to steal her. It’s that fun “Stranger Things” contrast.

Derek’s bedroom at the Turnbow house was a lot of fun. He’s like my spoiled little brother growing up, and everything I was jealous of, he had it. It was a little bit of a take on Francis from “Pee-wee’s Big Adventure”. Everything that happens in that house is so “Stranger Things”, with the kids all setting traps and doing their beats to catch the Demogorgon. I like the cultural life layer more than I do the pure sci-fi stuff, because it’s given me more to do.


Set decoration of “Stranger Things” by Jess Royal, courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: Where do you find this big grandfather clock that we see in the Upside Down?

Jess: I had a lot of options from eBay and different auctions. We needed some of the elements to be replicated, so we couldn’t have anything so unique and crazy that it would be too hard or time consuming to copy it. Once I found that one clock, that was it. It was traditional enough, but also big and imposing. I shared that with the Duffers and Chris, and they all loved it. I wish I had a more interesting story [laughs], but it was one of those you know it when you see it moments. I think it was in Michigan, and we bought it off eBay on auction, and had it transported down to Atlanta.

We were all careful with it on set. We would put it into a tree or a coffin, and we didn’t want anything to break. We had a few variations of it where they built it just in case, but it held together pretty well.


On the sets of “Stranger Things” with the grandfather clock. Courtesy of Jess Royal and Netflix.

Kirill: As they go into the Upside Down, they see the mirror “images” of their houses, the school and other places. How did you approach decorating these “other world” houses?

Jess: On most seasons it came up later. Going into it, I didn’t necessarily have a plan to replicate everything.

I found Eddie’s trailer in Florida, and had it shipped up. Then we found that it had asbestos in it, and we had to take all the asbestos out. I decorated it with this whole collection of trucker hats, and a whole collection of coffee mugs, and other stuff that was all over the trailer. It was almost a small house that we were creating. Then, after we had already started shooting, we found out that they were going to have to go in the Upside Down in his trailer.

It was a little bit forgiving, because the tentacles and the vines can help cover if there’s something I cannot find as an exact replica or a duplicate. It’s also flexible because the Upside Down was created at a moment in time in 1983. While certain things have changed in the real world over the years, you can go back to that original – what it would have been in 1983 in the Upside Down. By the time season five came around, I was already planning for everything to be seen in the Upside Down, trying to find at least two if not more of everything.

We didn’t even see the Wheeler house in the Upside Down until at least season three or maybe season four. A lot of that stuff ended up being covered with vines or painted over. Then the next season I had to try and clean it up when we saw the house back again in the Rightside Up. It was a trial and error process.


Set decoration of “Stranger Things” by Jess Royal, courtesy of Netflix.

Kirill: Are you by now used to walking away from these sets and spaces that you’ve decorated, spaces that have lived in your head for a full decade?

Jess: I think I handled it better than a lot of people. There are some people in other departments who came on just for season five. I saw some of them crying on the last night we were filming, and I was a little more bittersweet.

I’ve been planning for it for a long time. Originally, we were only going to do three seasons. When we were first setting up for season one, the Duffers said if people actually watch this, then we have a three season arc we’re thinking of. We’ll know what it is, and there’s an end point, and we can plan for that then. And as it got bigger and bigger, there was the push to have more content, so they expanded some storylines and we ended up going five seasons.

But mentally I’d always been prepared for three seasons. So by the time we got to season five, I was ready to move on and do other things. I would do anything with the Duffers always. They’re the best. But at least for this storyline and these characters, I felt like we watched them grow up and I liked the ending. I was OK with letting it go.


Design sketches for the “Scoops Ahoy” ice cream parlor on “Stranger Things”. Courtesy of Jess Royal and Netflix.

Kirill: Did you get to keep any piece to yourself for your personal collection?

Jess: Not anything that anybody would notice or care about. I kept a set of glasses from the Wheeler house. I have a firm “one in, one out” rule in my house. Working as a set decorator and being tempted to keep so much, I have to purge something else if I’m going to bring something into my house. There’s so much that people wanted, so I just let them have their pick, and I kept those glasses for myself.


On the sets of the Starcourt Mall of “Stranger Things”. Courtesy of Jess Royal and Netflix.

Kirill: How do you see the world of generative AI today in your industry?

Jess: It’s a hot topic. Last summer I worked on the movie “Artificial” about Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Ilya Sutskever who is one of the people who created OpenAI. I downloaded ChatGPT for that movie, because I felt that I should try and figure out how people were using it and what it was all about. But honestly, I deleted it after that movie and I have turned off every aspect of AI that you can on your phone, be it in search results or email summaries.

As far as technology goes, I’m old school. For a long time I thought that the Internet was just a trend and that it was going to go away eventually [laughs]. Obviously I was wrong on that. I still read books and I don’t like to read anything digitally. Of all people you would ask that question to, I’m hoping if there ever is a dark age again and technology falls by the wayside, I’ll be poised to do really well. I know how to use card catalogs and libraries and microfiche and all the old analog technology.

There are already actors and actresses that are being created by AI that people are embracing as real people, and it’s troubling. But there is a spot for a real physical person coming up with these concepts as a production designer or as a decorator in a lot of these productions – at least for now, until AI is so good that they can think our thoughts better than we can. As of right now, I feel like AI gets it wrong a lot of times, so there’s still definitely a need for human beings and creativity in that sense.


On the sets of the Soviet prison of “Stranger Things”. Courtesy of Jess Royal and Netflix.

Kirill: What are the key ingredients to longevity in this field?

Jess: It’s very important to start from the bottom and do it the hard way, and I believe in doing it the hard way. You can start as a PA and learn your craft watching other people do it well. I was a location scout, but I started even below that as a locations PA. I was cleaning out porta potties and honey wagons. And that was after finishing law school and practicing law, so I had to humble myself, take a step backwards, and watch other people do their jobs well. It also advised what I wanted to do specifically in the industry and how to do it well.

There was a period of time here in Atlanta when they were making so many movies and there was a need to have more crew in the union. People were saying that I don’t even have to start at the bottom. I can join the union now and start working. I think that was a missed opportunity for people to start and learn the industry from the ground up. A lot of the people I know who have left the industry now are people who went in too fast, did their thing for a couple years, and now they’ve had to go back to working in some other places.

Take your time. Be a small person observing for a while before you think yourself having made it in film.


On the sets of “Stranger Things”. Courtesy of Jess Royal and Netflix.

Kirill: What was your favorite dish that you had while you were working on “Stranger Things” in Lithuania?

Jess: The best place that we ate in Lithuania was a Mexican restaurant that was owned by a mixed couple – the wife was from Mexico City and then husband was from Vilnius in Lithuania. They opened this little adobe casa place right downtown near our hotel, and it was some of the best Mexican food I’ve ever had.


On the sets of “Stranger Things”. Courtesy of Jess Royal and Netflix.


On the sets of “Stranger Things”. Courtesy of Jess Royal and Netflix.


On the sets of “Stranger Things”. Courtesy of Jess Royal and Netflix.

And here I want to thank Jess Royal for sharing her time with me to talk about the art and craft of set decoration, and for sharing the supporting materials. I also want to thank Meghan Johnson for making this interview happen. All seasons of “Stranger Things” are streaming on Netflix. Finally, if you want to know more about how films and TV shows are made, click here for additional in-depth interviews in this series.

item.content:encoded:
Continuing the ongoing series of interviews with creative artists working on various aspects of movie and episodic productions, it is my pleasure to welcome Charlie Cole. In this interview, he talks about the transition of the industry from film to digital, the evolution of tools at his disposal, importance of communication, and his thoughts on generative AI. Between all these and more, Charlie takes a deep dive into his work on the just released “Cruel Hands”.


Charlie Cole on the set of “Cruel Hands”.

Kirill: Please tell us about yourself and the path that took you to where you are today.

Charlie: My name is Charlie Cole, and I’m a cinematographer. I started out as a fine artist, I was in love with charcoal drawing, and went to undergrad in Brooklyn at Pratt Institute. And then I realized that to be a fine artist, at least what worked for me, you’re isolating yourself in the world so much. I started falling in love with the idea of working with collaborators and being inspired by other people’s art forms, which led me to picking up a camera and seeing how that fit – and I just fell in love with that.

I did freelance director / cinematographer work for a couple years, experimental poetic narrative type things, and then I applied to this grad school in LA called American Film Institute for cinematography. That’s when I started taking it more seriously as far as a craft and a career. Before it was much more of a passion and something that I felt very in tune to – but now it’s full throttle, making my job, making my life fully cinematography.

Kirill: Would you call yourself a digital native? Did you catch the tail end of the film as the medium?

Charlie: I love that term digital native, that’s really fun. I was at the transitional period where film was still very much alive, but not being taught so much. I got my hands on it a little bit, but only enough to see how beautiful it was. It was never directly accessible to me easily.

Even today, if I ever want to shoot with film, it’s quite a challenge with production to get film going. I get maybe a year to shoot a project on film. Usually it’s a short or a commercial. I love film, but I’m a digital native for sure. I definitely grew up with it, and feel very comfortable with it.

Now everything is so good that you can cheat it so easily between the two. I did a music video years ago with the director of “Cruel Hands”, and we worked with Andre Chlebak, the colorist who did “Mandy”. I could have sworn that “Mandy” was on film. I would have bet an arm and leg on it. My first question was what film stock was used, and sure enough it was digital. And if you’ve ever seen Steve Yedlin videos, he shows you how you can make anything look like anything else with the right approach of digital control or manipulation.


Cinematography of “Cruel Hands” by Charlie Cole.

Kirill: What are the misunderstandings or misconceptions about cinematography?

Charlie: I’m half French and half American. When I tell my French side of the family what a cinematographer is, they’ve never heard of it. I think in Europe there’s a lot more of the idea that the author-artist is in charge of the story and the vision, including the camera work, especially in French cinema.

Our role as cinematographer changes culture to culture and depends on each collaboration with each director. I’ve seen collaborations where the cinematographer is more of a camera technician who is helping the director’s vision come alive, and those can work beautifully. I’ve seen collaborations where the cinematographer and the director are figuring it out together. I’ve seen and been in situations where directors come from more of a theater background or they have a wonderful idea with little film experience, and they’re using you to help finesse the story through filmmaking and how to show a story through a film. It can mean so many different things.

The term that I’ve come to love is that the cinematographer is shooting what the actors cannot say. Your job is to shoot the subtext of every performance and shoot the subtext of the story. Years ago I saw “Shawshank Redemption” on a plane, and I had no headphones, so I watched it on mute. But the whole time it was clear what was happening, what the characters were going through, and what the story was going towards. That’s the job of the cinematographer – that the images say everything that can’t be said otherwise.


Cinematography of “Cruel Hands” by Charlie Cole.

Kirill: What is the most exciting recent development technology-wise, or maybe the most exciting technical thing that is on the horizon in your area?

Charlie: AI is obviously an exciting conversation – or very scary, depending on how you look at it.

The most exciting thing for me these days is that every camera is pretty excellent. I’m an Amira owner, and it’s quite large. I often find myself wanting to have a smaller camera for a trick shot or whatever, and almost anything you use looks gorgeous. It opens up a lot of doors, both financially and aesthetically. You can put the camera anywhere, and you can pretty much do anything.

I grew up in a world where I was idolizing the big chunky cameras that I would see on film sets, and I wanted to get my hands on those. And now that’s fizzling apart. Now it’s about finding a way to get the perfect image any way we can.

Kirill: Getting to “Cruel Hands”, how did you find your way to it, or maybe how did it find its way to you?

Charlie: Al Kalyk, the director of “Cruel Hands”, is one of my best friends. We went to grad school at the American Film Institute together. It’s his first feature, and we’ve been talking about it for maybe a year and a half before the funding started coming in. There were many parts of it, and then it ended up being a wonderful thing that we had been collaborating for so long.

It was a fully Australian production, and I was the only American there. He had to fight for me to be able to be a part of it, because there was pressure to have full Australian crew, tax incentives being involved and all. He really stuck his neck out to bring me on, and I couldn’t have done it with a better person. He’s been one of my best friends for a long time, and a collaborator too. We’ve done a lot of music videos and shorts together.


From the lookbook of “Cruel Hands”, courtesy of Charlie Cole.

Kirill: What discussions did you have about the visual style of this story?

Charlie: The discussions led a lot around blending early Cohen brothers and 70s western films and the boldness of that camera work with a much a more delicate look to the film. Our look – the coloring and the way the lenses were showing the world – came from a place closer to “Phantom Thread”. Our story is a balance between a mother and son who are trying to get through a tough situation , and then this husband who is chasing them down. There’s this contradiction between a western thriller and a coming of age quieter film, so the film had to find a way to mix in between the two visually.

We had a ton of references between the two of us. When he first sent me the script, I sent him this big lookbook that was what you would expect from a film like this on script. It’s independent, it’s low contrast, it’s a very wide open lens kind of aesthetic. And then Al came back to me and said that it was all wrong and that we have to start from scratch. He wanted the bold western in there, which you don’t get often these days. I loved that.


From the lookbook of “Cruel Hands”, courtesy of Charlie Cole.

Kirill: How did you approach separating the flashbacks from the main storyline?

Charlie: That’s something that got discovered in post. We didn’t shoot chronologically, but that was intended to be the earlier part of the film. Al directed the film, and he was also the editor. In the editing table he discovered that it was a lot more interesting as a back and forth jumping between the narratives.

In this film we had an approach where the first act uses only wide angle lenses, so it was shot on Leica-Rs 14-22mm. Act two was 25-50mm, and act three was 50-110mm. This turns the film into a pressure cooker where the image is getting more and more compressed as the film goes on. And then now that we have the flashbacks, you feel the world encroaching upon you, and then all of a sudden you get this escape into a wide-lenses flashback. It does a good job at releasing tension when it needs to be.

Kirill: Was there any color that you wanted to stay away from?

Charlie: For whatever reason, it didn’t feel like there was any room for purples. Our world is blue and green by nature, because it was so much in the woods. Then there was a lot of yellow and a lot of red. The father character was always represented by red. He is this encroaching threat, so the only red we ever wanted to feel in the whole film was only what was associated with him. We only feel red when we’re in the flashbacks at the house which he has a large part of, and then we feel more as he gets close – towards the end of the film when we’re more and more surrounded by the wildfires. The sky turns red and so the whole third act of the film is entirely dosed in red – which hopefully feels like a foreboding of him coming and taking over.


Lighting diagram for “Cruel Hands”, courtesy of Charlie Cole.

Kirill: Was the house a single thing, or was it split between location and set builds?

Charlie: The house was one beautiful location. But the entire floorboard scene where we find this big cavity under the house where the mother and son end up hiding underneath during the film – that was entirely built on the same property as the house. We had to have scenes where they’re crawling into it from the interior location, so we ended up building a six inch platform that covered the whole floor of additional wood that they could then break and go into. It was pretty intensive.

We were shooting with the Alexa Mini LF, which is not too big and not too small. Luckily, because that scene was a separate build, we’re in a barn at that point, so the camera was just right aligned with them. We were about five feet off the ground to give them the proper staging that they needed to climb up into it. Luckily we didn’t have to sneak a camera into a little cavity.

Kirill: What was your lighting setup? How are the lights treating you these days?

Charlie: We had a great gaffer named Dan Michaud and a great key grip named Sean Aston. It was a pretty small team all things considered. Our budget wasn’t too big on this, and the lighting was a lot of hustle. It was all LED, a lot of sky panels, a lot of little kino tubes here and there for little beats.

We were trying to primarily light from outside the windows as much as possible, because the space wasn’t very big. We had a lot of 360 situations going on in there, but we were fortunate that our location had this big cavity above us, like an A-frame. So Dan was able to sneak in a ton of little spotlights above, which helped us get this more western cinematic feeling. If the light were through the windows, it would have been so naturalistic and beautiful in its own right, but to really get that punchy high contrast effect we had to have all these little spotlights all over the place. That way you have these little moments that characters would step into.


Lighting diagram for “Cruel Hands”, courtesy of Charlie Cole.

Kirill: You said that the cameras are pretty great these days. What about the lights? Is there room for improvement there?

Charlie: Lights are so great these days. About 5-6 years ago when I was starting to do more serious work and play with a wider range of LEDs, there was a lot of difficulty with CRI [color rendition index] and the fidelity. If something says it’s red, is it actually red? All these different lights would be all the different flavors of red. Now everything is pretty wonderful. You can get battery packed lights and throw them all over the place, and it allows you to do so much.

My last feature film is called “Corpus”, and it just premiered at Fantasia last week. That film is a ’90s period film and we only used tungsten and HMI lights to keep it period-relevant. It was a challenge, or rather a burden of love. It gave us a lot of interesting images. What I noticed most with tungsten lights is that compared to LEDs they tend to punch stronger. If you’re looking at a skin tone, it seems a little bit richer and a little bit denser. It’s almost like it pierces the first layer of skin and hits a little harder. You can’t beat a nice tungsten for that beautiful close-up, but the practicality of it is a thing.

Kirill: Is it a little bit painful to not have full control over how people see it? We have so many screens in our lives after the movie is out of theaters – laptops, tablets, phones, and those tiny plane screens that you mentioned earlier.

Charlie: If I tried to fix that, I would lose my mind [laughs]. It’s impossible. The only thing I could ever do is if I’m showing it to a friend, I get to their house 10 minutes early and mess up all their TV settings. For me, the most color correct home theater setup is when I check it on a MacBook, as they are so good.

It is difficult. It is heartbreaking. But at the end of the day, there’s only so much you can do. You color it for the theater. You color one more time for a MacBook. And then beyond that you have to let the world be what the world is. Hopefully, if somebody’s watching on whatever TV they have in their house, they’re watching everything that way. That’s how they watch “Dune” and every other movie. Their level is already standardized and hopefully they’re not comparing theatrical “Dune” to your movie at home.


Cinematography of “Cruel Hands” by Charlie Cole.

Kirill: What went into the fire sequence at the end?

Charlie: Around 90% of the smoke is all practical in the film. We had a bunch of PAs who were slogging large tubes full of haze all over the fields. Then we had them stay around the area so that if the wind ever changed direction on us, we could compensate by having haze come from another way. They rocked.

We had very little fire, either one or two flame bars that we use as references. Other than that, if we had a close-up of somebody during a fire scene, we’d put the flame bar right under the camera. That way you get the heat effect, and also feel it in their eyes. That’s something that is harder to fake with VFX. Other than that it was a really great job from the VFX team. We’d put a flame bar somewhere, and they would use it as a reference to throw it all over the scene. When I look at it now, I know there was no fire there, and it just looks amazing. They did such a great job.


Cinematography of “Cruel Hands” by Charlie Cole.

Kirill: Is there such a thing as the most challenging day or sequence that you had on this production?

Charlie: We had a lot of obstacles. The story of the film turns into being surrounded by wildfires, and we had to have the feeling that the air is always full of smoke. That meant that we could never have any direct sunlight once the fires have started. So in order to get the sky light correct at our location in Australia, we could only shoot at dusk or dawn, or when it was extremely cloudy, or when the sun went behind a mountain. We were shooting in this big valley, so that limited us extremely in terms of when we could shoot any outdoor scenes during the third act of the film.

We were in Australia, so we had monsoons, we had snakes, we had venomous spiders. One day it was night shoot with Diesel La Torraca who was about 12 years old at the time, and our key grip discovered a brown snake, which is the second most venomous snake in Australia. If you get bit, you die in 30 minutes, and the nearest hospital is 30 minutes away [laughs]. So we had to have a snake wrangler come in and check the whole property. He found a whole nest of them. It’s a crazy place.

There was a scene where we’re shooting them running in the woods. We had a two camera setup. I was on one camera and Al the director was on the other camera. They have these 1.5 inch long bull ants, and if they bite you, it’s extremely painful. Al was sitting on this apple box, and one of our grips was swiping ants off of his back because they were crawling up [laughs]. It was stuff like that every day.

We also got rained into location several times. One time we were there for about four hours because we literally couldn’t leave. We were flooded in. It was a wild shoot. I’ve never experienced anything like that. But it adds to the energy of the film. You really have to fight for it. And the craziest thing is that the rest of our otherwise fully Australian crew was just used to it. I have this video of myself in the car with a camera, and I look to the right, and there’s a huge python right outside the car just going across the street. And everybody else was just taking a minute until it was gone [laughs]. It’s a special but wild place.


Cinematography of “Cruel Hands” by Charlie Cole.

Kirill: Why should people go to see this movie on the big screen in the movie theater?

Charlie: We shot the film on the Mini LF, so the film is in large format. You really get a sense of space the way we shot this film. Space is so important for this project. You feel the claustrophobia of the cabin that they’re in, and then you have the vastness of the fire that surrounds them later. It’s a cinematic film. We had this incredible composer Libby Hsieh who goes by their artist name Alvidrez, and the sound design of this film is amazing. There’s breath work and crackling of fire and haunting instrumental crackling. It’s a special soundscape.

Kirill: Where do you find yourself these days on the raging debates around generative AI?

Charlie: I’ve been going back and forth with all of it. On one hand, any tool is a wonderful thing to have at your disposal. On the other hand, it is unfortunate that this tool is frankly based off of a lot of other people’s work – and that it’s gotten so good that you can replace work.

Career wise, it is a huge disappointment that it is replacing a lot of smaller jobs. If you’re shooting a shoe commercial or a food commercial, those things are easily replaceable now with AI. And those are the bread and butter of how people stay working so we can do fun projects like this – and also how you learn new tools and how you learn your craft. That’s where you finesse your abilities, and that is going out the window.


Cinematography of “Cruel Hands” by Charlie Cole.

Kirill: What are the ingredients for longevity in this industry?

Charlie: I can only speak to what’s worked for me. Something that I’ve found to be helpful for my approach as a cinematographer is that I come from fine arts. Teachers would always say that everybody in the room can draw, and then ask “Why are you drawing?”

I see the same issue or the same thought process with a camera. Anybody knows how to expose. What makes you holding the camera or lighting the scene different from other people’s abilities to do the same thing? That goes in terms of your personal flavor, and how emotionally involved you are into the work you do, and your collaboration with your director and the actors and crewmates.

The short answer is that the key to longevity is in who you are as a person. If you’re kind, if you’re generous, and if you’re genuine, you will go far. You have to lend your heart and your eyes to everything you do.


Cinematography of “Cruel Hands” by Charlie Cole.

Kirill: Is there a piece of advice you’d want to give to your younger self?

Charlie: I’ve had a lot of good fortune with working with people that I really love and that are quite different from me. So my advice would be to make sure I continue to do that – work with as many different people who care as adamantly as you do. There’s nothing better than people who come from different backgrounds and different experiences and different desires of what the film is and could be – as long as we all put all of our heart into it every chance we get. Then we’re all going to make something special.

The other advice would be to communicate, communicate, communicate. That’s a lesson I learned over time. People speak different languages in terms of what images are. I worked with this director who I went to AFI with, and she came from a theater background, while my parents are architects. When we started working together, we started talking about wide shots and we talked for weeks about those wide shots. Then we got on to set, and in my mind the wide shot is the person defined by space, defined by the architecture. And in her mind, a wide shot was a head-to-toe shot of a person, because she works with actors.

I realized that we have been speaking in completely different languages for two or three months now [laughs], but we never thought to compare it with specific images. That’s a lesson that I’ve learned the hard way – make sure you’re on the same page before you get to set. Even though it feels like it, you never know. It’s as simple as referencing images. When I say wide, I mean this. Yes, we’re on the same page. When I say close up, I mean this. Yes, we’re on the same page. When I say cool, I mean cobalt blue and not light blue. When I say red, I mean fiery angry red and not calm red. People have so many different tastes, so locking in on that is extremely important.

As far as prep goes, one of my favorite things ever on any film set is that moment where you and the director are so in sync, that if, God forbid, one of you is in an accident or is sick and has to miss a day, the director would trust that you would run every shot and every setup the exact way that you guys had talked about. That’s where you want to be when you hop onto a film set.

Kirill: When you turn on the TV, what would be a movie that you would watch again and again, no questions asked, whenever it comes on?

Charlie: “Lord of The Rings” no doubt. I’m such a fantasy guy. I watch so many movies. I love to be entertained. I love to watch movies that transcend me.

Films that I admire are different from films that I watch. If I see a film that pushes me artistically or inspires me artistically, I try not to watch it again. So much depends on who you were when you saw it, and how you were feeling that day when you saw it. If it really affected you, watching it again would potentially ruin it or take away the magic of what you experienced. It lives in your soul and I don’t want to analyze it. Those are films by Lynne Ramsay, Lars von Trier, Gaspar Noe. They stick with me artistically, and I try not to watch them anymore.

For the films that I would watch again and again, pretty much anything science fiction or fantasy. You have to probably pull me away if it was on the TV. I watched all of the “Pirates of the Caribbean” yesterday. It was a great day [laughs].


Cinematography of “Cruel Hands” by Charlie Cole.

Kirill: Is it difficult for you to enjoy the story and not overanalyze it from the cinematography perspective?

Charlie: The better the cinematography and the better the filmmaking is, the less distracted I get from it. For sure, any of us who work in this industry are analyzing things and picking up on things all the time. If they are masters of the craft, you just forget. How impressive is it to trick people who are there to analyze into forgetting any of that? It takes a really great film for me to completely forget that I’m watching a film, and they’re few and far in between. I love those.

That being said, I still love seeing how the sausage is made. I get a big kick out of that. Maybe it means that the film is lacking in something, and then I get inspired by something else. Usually I’m noticing the good stuff.

Kirill: What was your favorite dish in Australia that you had while working on “Cruel Hands”?

Charlie: All of the food in Australia was impeccable. There was this meat pie that I loved. I was living in Los Angeles at the time, and I’d have avocado toast constantly. There was this place in Australia that I would go to almost every weekend that I could to have avocado toast, because the food there was so fresh and prepared with so much care. They also sell the Maxibon brand of ice cream, and I probably had 500 of them during the three months I was there [laughs]. It was a whole thing. They sell them at gas stations everywhere, and it was the best thing I had there. I got really obsessed with those.

And here I want to thank Charlie Cole for sharing his time with me to talk about the art and craft of cinematography, and for sharing the supporting materials. I also want to thank Jordan von Netzer for making this interview happen. “Cruel Hands” is out now streaming on Apple, YouTube and Amazon. Finally, if you want to know more about how films and TV shows are made, click here for additional in-depth interviews in this series.

item.content:encoded:
I’m pleased to announce the next major release of Aurora. The two main themes of this release are:

  • Expanding on the foundational work of the previous releases around color tokens, painters and shapers
  • The introduction of a brand new skin, Blueprint (image above)

Among the many other new features and bug fixes in this release:

  • Introduction of component shapers that replace the previously available button shapers and expand the scope to all components
  • Revisited API surface of decoration painters, folding the overlay painters to be managed by decoration painters, and introducing the brand new inlay painters
  • Unified visuals of tab buttons and newly added tab decorators that allow custom visuals of tabs
  • New color tokens for marker-on-container and container-shadow
  • New window decorators
  • Alphas for color tokens under enabled states
  • Additional customization options for title panes for button icons and title texts
  • Improve contrast and fidelity of icon filtering

Aurora focuses on helping you make elegant and high-performing desktop applications in Compose. If you’re in the business of writing just such apps, I’d love for you to take this Aurora release for a spin.
